question: In what year did the storming of the Bastille take place?
document: The storming of the Bastille took place on 14 July, when crowds in Paris attacked the medieval fortress on the eastern edge of the city. The Bastille had long served as a state prison, and to many Parisians it symbolized the arbitrary power of the monarchy under Louis XVI. Tension in the capital had been building for weeks. The Estates-General had opened at Versailles in May, and in June the deputies of the Third Estate declared themselves a National Assembly and swore the Tennis Court Oath, promising not to disband until France had a constitution. When the king dismissed the popular finance minister Jacques Necker and royal troops gathered around Paris, rumors spread that the Assembly would be crushed. On the morning of the attack, crowds seized tens of thousands of muskets from the Invalides and then marched on the Bastille in search of gunpowder. The governor, Bernard-René de Launay, eventually surrendered after several hours of fighting, during which about a hundred attackers were killed. De Launay was then murdered, and his head was paraded through the streets on a pike. Only seven prisoners were found inside. The fortress was demolished over the following months, and some of its stones were carved into souvenir models. The anniversary of the attack is now celebrated as France's national holiday.

question: Which Portuguese navigator commanded the first European voyage to reach India by sailing around Africa, arriving in 1498?
document: Portugal's search for a sea route to Asia had been building for most of the fifteenth century. Under the patronage of Prince Henry the Navigator, Portuguese captains pushed steadily down the west coast of Africa, and in 1488 Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of the continent, proving that the Atlantic connected to the Indian Ocean. King Manuel I then commissioned a fleet of four ships to complete the journey. The expedition left Lisbon in July 1497 and, instead of hugging the African coast, swung far out into the South Atlantic to catch favorable winds, spending about three months out of sight of land. After rounding the Cape of Good Hope, the fleet worked its way up the east African coast, meeting hostility at Mozambique and Mombasa but finding a friendly reception at Malindi, where it took on a pilot familiar with the monsoon routes. The ships crossed the Arabian Sea and anchored near Calicut on the Malabar Coast. Negotiations with the local ruler, the Zamorin, were strained, partly because the Portuguese gifts seemed paltry to a court accustomed to rich trade. The return voyage was grueling; scurvy killed many of the crew, and only two ships made it back to Lisbon. Even so, the cargo of spices was enough to show the immense profits the new route could bring.

question: Which river forms much of the border between Texas and Mexico?
document: The international boundary between the United States and Mexico runs for roughly 3,100 kilometres from the Gulf of Mexico to the Pacific Ocean, and more than half of that length lies along the southern edge of Texas. The line was largely established by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, which ended the Mexican-American War in 1848, and was adjusted by the Gadsden Purchase a few years later. West of El Paso, the border crosses open desert in New Mexico, Arizona and California, where it is marked by fences, monuments and surveyed straight lines. In Texas, by contrast, the boundary follows a natural feature, which has caused periodic disputes when floods shifted its channel; the long-running Chamizal dispute between El Paso and Ciudad Juarez was not settled until 1963. The Texas section passes a series of paired twin cities, including Laredo and Nuevo Laredo, McAllen and Reynosa, and Brownsville and Matamoros, which are linked by dozens of bridges carrying trade, commuters and tourists. Big Bend National Park, in a remote stretch of the Chihuahuan Desert, encloses spectacular canyons such as Santa Elena, where cliffs rise some 450 metres. The International Boundary and Water Commission, which took its modern form in 1944, manages dams and water-sharing agreements along the frontier.

question: In what year was the Battle of Waterloo fought?
document: The Battle of Waterloo was fought on 18 June near the village of Waterloo, south of Brussels in what is now Belgium. It pitted Napoleon Bonaparte, who had escaped from exile on the island of Elba and returned to power in France, against two allied armies: an Anglo-allied force commanded by the Duke of Wellington and a Prussian army under Field Marshal Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher. Two days earlier, Napoleon had defeated the Prussians at Ligny, but Blücher's army withdrew in good order rather than retreating eastward, which allowed it to march to Wellington's aid. On the day of the battle, heavy overnight rain delayed the French attack until late morning. Wellington's troops held a ridge and defended the farmhouses of Hougoumont and La Haye Sainte against repeated assaults, including massed French cavalry charges against infantry squares. In the evening, as Prussian columns pressed on the French right flank at Plancenoit, Napoleon committed the Imperial Guard, whose repulse caused the French army to collapse. Wellington later called the battle the nearest-run thing you ever saw in your life. Napoleon abdicated for the second time a few days later and was exiled to the remote island of Saint Helena in the South Atlantic.

question: Who served as the first Chancellor of the German Empire after its unification in 1871?
document: The German Empire was proclaimed on 18 January 1871 at a ceremony held in occupied France, while the Franco-Prussian War was still drawing to a close and Paris remained under siege. King Wilhelm I of Prussia was declared German Emperor, and the southern German states of Bavaria, Württemberg, Baden and Hesse joined the North German Confederation to form a single federal state dominated by Prussia. Unification had been achieved through three short wars: against Denmark in 1864, against Austria in 1866, and against France in 1870 and 1871. The Prussian minister-president who had steered these conflicts became the head of the new imperial government. In domestic affairs his government waged the Kulturkampf against the political influence of the Catholic Church, passed anti-socialist laws, and at the same time introduced pioneering social insurance programs covering sickness, accidents, old age and disability. In foreign policy he sought to isolate France and keep the peace among the great powers through a complex web of alliances, including the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary and the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia. He also hosted the Congress of Berlin in 1878, which redrew the map of the Balkans. After the young Wilhelm II came to the throne, the two men clashed over policy, and the chancellor was forced to resign in 1890.

question: Which Scottish engineer invented the separate condenser that greatly improved the efficiency of the steam engine?
document: Before the separate condenser, the dominant steam engine was the atmospheric engine designed by Thomas Newcomen in the early eighteenth century and used mainly to pump water out of mines. In that design, steam filled a cylinder and was then condensed by a spray of cold water inside the same cylinder, creating a partial vacuum so that atmospheric pressure pushed the piston down. The method was enormously wasteful, because the cylinder had to be reheated with fresh steam after every stroke. The decisive insight came in 1765, reportedly during a Sunday walk on Glasgow Green, after a model Newcomen engine had been brought in for repair at the University of Glasgow. The solution was to condense the steam in a separate vessel, kept permanently cold, while the main cylinder stayed hot. Fuel consumption fell by roughly three quarters. Turning the idea into reliable machinery took years. A partnership with the Birmingham manufacturer Matthew Boulton supplied capital and skilled workers, and John Wilkinson's precise cylinder-boring technique made it possible to build tight-fitting pistons. Later refinements included the sun-and-planet gear, which converted reciprocating motion into rotary motion, and the centrifugal governor for regulating engine speed.
